title: What SANS is
summary: In weightlessness, blood and cerebrospinal fluid shift toward the head. This can cause optic nerve swelling, folds in the retina, flattening of the back of the eye and brain swelling, together called SANS. Some astronauts have only mild changes, others clinically significant ones; risk is higher on longer missions and the long-term outcome is not known.
document: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)

title: How SANS is monitored in flight
summary: In-flight monitoring described by NASA includes a vision questionnaire (changes in vision and symptoms such as headache, rated mild, moderate or severe), visual acuity testing, an Amsler grid where wavy, blurred or missing lines count as positive, and eye imaging (optical coherence tomography, fundoscopy and ultrasound) guided from the ground. A questionnaire cannot replace these examinations.
document: Evidence Report: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)

title: Eye imaging during long missions
summary: In a study of 11 astronauts, optical coherence tomography was performed in flight around flight days 10 to 150; the vascular layer around the optic nerve (peripapillary choroid) thickened during flight. Imaging results are interpreted by specialists.
source_name: Macias, Patel, Gibson et al., JAMA Ophthalmology
document: Association of long-duration spaceflight with anterior and posterior ocular structure changes in astronauts and their recovery

title: Sleep loss and irregular schedules in spaceflight
summary: Astronauts face work overload, irregular light-dark cycles and disrupted sleep. NASA describes sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload as a risk to performance and health. The ISS uses LED lighting that simulates an Earth-like light-dark cycle.
document: Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules

title: Short sleep and attention
summary: NASA's Human Research Roadmap notes that crews sleep about six hours a night and that chronically sleeping around six hours leads to decrements in vigilant attention. This relationship is established mainly in ground studies.
document: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

title: How sleep has been measured on the ISS
summary: A study of 64 Shuttle and 21 ISS astronauts used wrist actigraphy worn continuously and a daily computerized sleep log; average sleep on the ISS was about six hours. A 3-minute reaction-time self-test (psychomotor vigilance test) has also been used on the ISS to measure alertness.
source_name: Barger, Flynn-Evans et al., Lancet Neurology
document: Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts before, during, and after spaceflight

title: Isolation, confinement and mood
summary: NASA describes that prolonged isolation and confinement can increase the risk of behavioral issues and psychiatric disorders such as anxiety and depression, and can affect sleep, morale and decision making. Communication delays on long missions are a new challenge.
document: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders

title: Cognitive self-tests used in spaceflight
summary: The Cognition test battery has 10 short tests (including a 3-minute reaction-time test), takes about 18 minutes on a laptop or tablet, and has been used on the ISS. Results are compared with the same person's earlier sessions.
source_name: Basner et al., Aerospace Medicine and Human Performance
document: Development and Validation of the Cognition Test Battery for Spaceflight

title: Bone loss in weightlessness
summary: NASA reports that weight-bearing bones lose on average 1 to 1.5 percent of their density each month during four-to-six-month missions, which raises susceptibility to fractures. Resistive exercise reduces post-flight bone density deficits; bone scans are done before and after flight.

title: What can and cannot be measured for bone in flight
summary: According to NASA's bone loss technical brief, no system measures bone density in flight; density is measured with DXA scans before and after flight and every three years. The countermeasure goal is to keep hip and spine density at or above 95 percent of pre-mission values (90 percent for the femoral neck). Exercise devices record training data in flight.
source_name: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer

title: Resistive exercise and bone
summary: In a small flight study (13 astronauts), crew members using the advanced resistive exercise device kept hip and pelvis bone density near pre-flight levels, unlike crews with an older device. This is an association in a small group, not proof for an individual.
source_name: Smith, Heer, Shackelford et al., Journal of Bone and Mineral Research
document: Benefits for bone from resistance exercise and nutrition in long-duration spaceflight

title: Radiation exposure and cancer risk
summary: NASA explains that astronauts receive more radiation than people on Earth, which can lead to certain cancers and may also affect the heart, blood vessels, eyes and cognition. Instruments on the ISS measure radiation exposure. Measuring dose estimates long-term risk; it does not detect cancer.

title: NASA career radiation limit
summary: NASA's space flight standard sets an individual crew member's total career effective radiation dose from spaceflight below 600 millisieverts, the same for all ages and sexes, and requires keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable.
source_name: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
document: Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection - Technical Brief (quoting NASA-STD-3001)

title: How radiation is monitored on the ISS
summary: NASA's Space Radiation Analysis Group describes a personal Crew Active Dosimeter whose data reach ISS laptops and the ground, and area monitors; one monitor acts as an alarm when the dose rate exceeds a level where the crew may need to shelter.
source_name: NASA Johnson Space Center, Space Radiation Analysis Group
document: How do we protect the astronauts from space radiation?
